title: Cloud Computing and Green Computing
summary: What really happens when you save to "the cloud": cloud service models, what's inside a data centre, how cloud services scale and sometimes fail, how to keep cloud data secure, the energy and water cost of computing and AI, and practical ways to make computing greener.
learn: What cloud computing is and the main cloud service models
What's inside a data centre and how it is kept running
How cloud services scale, and why outages happen
How to keep data in the cloud secure and backed up
The environmental impact of data centres and AI
Practical ways to make computing greener
intro: Every message, stream, game and AI chat runs on computers in giant buildings called data centres. The cloud lets anyone use huge computing power on demand, but it also uses enormous amounts of electricity and water, especially as AI grows. In this topic you'll find out what the cloud really is, look inside a data centre, discover how services scale to millions of users (and what happens when they crash), learn to keep cloud data safe, and explore how computing can become greener.

pages.title: What is the cloud?
pages.spec: Define cloud computing, describe IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, and evaluate the cloud's advantages and disadvantages
pages.summary: Cloud computing means using computing services such as storage, software and processing power over the internet, from servers owned by a provider, instead of on your own device. Services are often grouped as SaaS, PaaS and IaaS.
pages.starter: "The cloud is just someone else's computer." Is this true? Discuss.
sc: I can describe SaaS, PaaS and IaaS with examples
I can evaluate advantages and disadvantages of using the cloud

b: Cloud computing: using storage, software and processing over the internet
Runs on servers in data centres owned by cloud providers
Big providers: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud
You rent what you need instead of buying your own hardware
SaaS (Software as a Service): use a finished app, e.g. Google Docs, Microsoft 365, Spotify
PaaS (Platform as a Service): a platform to build and run your own apps
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): rent virtual servers, storage and networks
Think pizza: eat out (SaaS), takeaway (PaaS), buy ingredients (IaaS)
Access from anywhere, on any device
Easy sharing and collaboration
No need to buy and maintain servers; pay for what you use
But: needs internet, depends on the provider, privacy and ongoing costs

blocks.text: What is cloud computing?

**[[cloud computing|Cloud computing]]** means using computing services (storage, software, processing power) over the internet instead of on your own device. The work is done by a **[[server]]**, a powerful computer that provides services to other computers, in a data centre owned by a cloud provider. The biggest providers are Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.
Cloud service models

blocks.caption: Cloud service models
head: Model
What you get
You manage
Examples
rows: A finished app you use through a browser or app
A platform for building and running your own apps
Virtual servers, storage and networking to rent

blocks.text: The pizza analogy: SaaS is eating at a restaurant (everything's done for you), PaaS is takeaway (you provide the table and plates), IaaS is buying the ingredients and using someone else's kitchen.
Advantages and disadvantages

blocks.caption: Weighing up the cloud
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Access files and apps from anywhere, on any device
You depend on the provider staying online and in business
Privacy: your data is on someone else's computers
No expensive hardware to buy; pay for what you use
Ongoing subscription costs can add up
Scale up instantly when you need more
Moving to another provider can be hard ("lock-in")

pages.title: Inside a data centre
pages.spec: Describe what is inside a data centre and how it is kept cool, powered and running
pages.summary: A data centre is a building full of servers, storage and networking equipment in racks. It needs huge amounts of power, cooling to remove heat, backup systems so it keeps running, and strong physical security. New AI data centres are packed with powerful GPUs.
pages.starter: Your laptop gets hot when you game. Imagine 100,000 computers in one building: what problems would you need to solve?
sc: I can describe the main parts of a data centre
I can explain why cooling and backup power are needed
I can explain redundancy and why data centres are built where they are

b: Rows of racks: tall cabinets holding many servers
Storage systems holding enormous amounts of data
High-speed networking connects everything to the internet
AI data centres: thousands of GPUs for training and running AI
Power: as much electricity as a town; backup batteries and generators
Cooling: fans, chilled air, water cooling, even liquid cooling directly on chips
Redundancy: spare parts and copies so one failure doesn't stop the service
Security: fences, guards, cameras, ID checks, fire suppression
Near cheap, reliable (ideally renewable) electricity
Cool climates reduce cooling costs
Good fibre connections and low risk of floods
Ireland hosts many data centres: they use about a fifth of its electricity

blocks.text: What is a data centre?

A **[[data centre]]** is a building that houses large numbers of servers, storage devices and networking equipment. Servers are mounted in tall metal cabinets called **[[rack|racks]]**, arranged in long rows. The largest data centres contain hundreds of thousands of servers.
New AI data centres are packed with GPUs (graphics processing units), chips that are very good at the maths AI needs. They use far more power per rack than ordinary servers.
Keeping a data centre running

blocks.caption: Data centre systems
head: System
Why it's needed
How it works
rows: Grid connection plus backup batteries (UPS) and diesel or battery generators
Computers turn electricity into heat, which damages them
Cold air flows through "cold aisles"; hot air is removed; some use water or liquid cooling on chips
Connects servers to each other and the internet
Fences, guards, CCTV, ID cards, fingerprint scanners
Special gases or mist that put fires out

blocks.text: Redundancy and uptime

**[[redundancy|Redundancy]]** means having spare equipment and copies of data so that if something fails, something else takes over. Data centres have redundant power supplies, network links and storage. Big providers copy data between data centres in different places, in case a whole building goes offline.
**[[uptime|Uptime]]** is the percentage of time a service is working. Cloud providers often promise "99.99% uptime", which still allows nearly an hour of downtime per year.

blocks.title: What does 99.9% uptime mean?
blocks.context: There are 8,760 hours in a year.
steps: 0.1% of 8,760 hours = 8.76 hours.
blocks.answer: 99.9% uptime still allows almost 9 hours offline a year. 99.99% allows about 53 minutes.

blocks.text: Location matters

Data centres are built where there is cheap, reliable electricity (ideally renewable), a cool climate, fast fibre connections and low risk of flooding or earthquakes. Ireland has become a major data-centre hub: data centres now use around a fifth of the Republic of Ireland's electricity, which has caused debate about pressure on the grid.

blocks.title: Build a data centre
steps: Your company wants to build a data centre on the island of Ireland. Look at the four site cards (power supply, climate, flood risk, fibre, local community).
Score each site and choose the best one.
Design the cooling, power and security systems for your data centre.
Write one way your data centre could benefit the local community.

q.q: Which site did you choose, and why?
q.a: E.g. the site with renewable wind power nearby, low flood risk and good fibre links, even if land costs more, because power and reliability matter most.

q.q: How could the data centre benefit the community?
q.a: E.g. pipe waste heat to warm nearby homes, schools or a swimming pool; create local jobs; invest in renewable energy.

check.q: What is a rack in a data centre?
o: A tall cabinet holding many servers

check.q: Why do data centres need cooling?
o: Servers turn electricity into heat that can damage them

check.q: What is redundancy?
o: Spare equipment and copies so a failure doesn't stop the service

check.q: What does 99.9% uptime allow per year?

practice.q: Describe three systems needed to keep a data centre running.
practice.a: Any three: power with backup (1); cooling (1); networking (1); security (1); fire suppression (1).

practice.q: Explain why a company might build a data centre in a cool country.
practice.a: Less energy needed for cooling (1), reducing cost and environmental impact (1).

pages.title: Scaling and outages
pages.spec: Explain virtualisation and scalability, and describe causes and effects of cloud outages
pages.summary: Virtualisation lets one physical server run many virtual machines, and cloud services scale up and down automatically to match demand. But because so many services share the same cloud providers, one fault can cause a huge outage affecting millions of people.
pages.starter: A concert sells tickets online at 9am and two million fans log on at once. What could go wrong?
sc: I can explain scalability and elasticity
I can describe causes and impacts of cloud outages

b: One physical server can run many virtual machines (VMs)
Each VM acts like a separate computer with its own operating system
Makes better use of hardware: less waste
Containers are a lighter-weight version
Scalability: handling more users by adding resources
Elasticity: scaling automatically up and down with demand
Load balancers share traffic between many servers
Pay only for what you use: ideal for ticket sales, Black Friday, exam results day
Outages are caused by software bugs, bad updates, configuration mistakes, power cuts or cyber attacks
Many apps rely on the same few providers, so one fault spreads
October 2025: a fault in one AWS region took down many popular apps and websites for hours
Resilience: spread services across regions and providers

blocks.text: Virtualisation

**[[virtualisation|Virtualisation]]** uses software to split one physical server into many **[[virtual machine|virtual machines]]** (VMs). Each VM behaves like a separate computer with its own operating system and programs. This means the hardware is used much more efficiently: instead of many half-empty servers, a few busy ones do the same work.
Scalability and elasticity

**[[scalability|Scalability]]** is a system's ability to handle more work by adding resources. Cloud services can be **elastic**: they automatically add servers when demand rises and remove them when it falls. A **[[load balancer]]** spreads incoming requests across many servers so none gets overloaded.

blocks.caption: Scaling in action
head: Event
What happens
Cloud response
rows: Millions of users arrive at once
Add hundreds of servers; use a virtual queue
Scale up for the morning, back down by afternoon
Scale down to save money and energy

blocks.text: Outages

An **[[outage]]** is when a service stops working. Causes include software bugs, faulty updates, configuration mistakes, power failures, cyber attacks and natural disasters. Because thousands of companies rely on the same few cloud providers, one fault can affect millions of people. In October 2025, a fault in one Amazon Web Services region caused many popular apps, games and websites to fail for hours around the world.

blocks.title: Building resilient services
items: Run copies of services in more than one region (so one failing area doesn't stop everything)
Test what happens when parts fail
Have backups and a plan for restoring them
Roll out updates gradually, not to everyone at once
Avoid relying on a single provider for critical services

blocks.title: Outage response team
steps: Read the incident report: "Ticketing site crashed for 3 hours during a big concert sale."
Identify what probably went wrong (use the scaling and outage notes).
Write a timeline of what the team should do during the outage.
Write three changes to stop it happening again.

q.a: Demand far exceeded capacity: the site didn't scale up fast enough, there was no virtual queue, and the database became overloaded.

q.q: Write three changes to prevent it next time.
q.a: E.g. pre-scale servers before the sale; use a load balancer and virtual queue; run copies in more than one region; load-test in advance with simulated users.

check.q: What is virtualisation?
o: Running many virtual machines on one physical server

check.q: What does elasticity mean in cloud computing?
o: Scaling up and down automatically with demand

check.q: What does a load balancer do?
Why can one cloud fault affect millions of people?
o: Many services rely on the same providers

practice.a: Many VMs on one server (1), so hardware is used more efficiently/less energy and cost (1).

practice.q: Describe how a cloud service could cope with a sudden rise in users.
practice.a: Automatically add servers/scale up (1); load balancer spreads traffic (1); virtual queue/scale back down afterwards (1).

pages.title: Securing the cloud
pages.spec: Describe how to keep data in the cloud secure, including shared responsibility, access control and backups
pages.summary: Keeping cloud data safe is a shared responsibility: providers secure the infrastructure, but users must protect their accounts, control sharing and back up important data. Strong passwords, two-factor authentication, encryption and the 3-2-1 backup rule all help.
pages.starter: You've shared a Google Drive folder with "Anyone with the link". Who could see it?
sc: I can explain the shared responsibility model
I can describe ways to secure cloud accounts and sharing
I can apply the 3-2-1 backup rule

b: The provider secures the buildings, hardware and network
You secure your account, passwords and sharing settings
Most cloud data leaks are caused by mistakes, e.g. files shared publicly by accident
Security is a team effort
Strong, unique passwords (or passkeys)
Two-factor authentication (2FA)
Check sharing: specific people, not "anyone with the link"
Watch for phishing emails pretending to be your cloud provider
3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, on 2 different types of storage, 1 off-site
Sync is not backup: deleting a file can delete it everywhere
Encryption protects data stored and sent
Data sovereignty: which country's laws apply to where your data is stored

blocks.text: Shared responsibility

In the **[[shared responsibility]]** model, the cloud provider protects the physical data centres, hardware and network, while the customer is responsible for their own accounts, passwords, settings and who they share data with. Many data leaks happen not because the cloud was hacked, but because someone set a folder or database to "public" by mistake.
Protecting your account

blocks.title: Cloud security habits
items: Use a strong, unique password or a passkey
Turn on **[[two-factor authentication]]** (2FA): a code or approval on your phone as well as your password
Share with specific people, not "anyone with the link", and remove access when it's no longer needed
Check sign-in alerts and recent activity
Beware phishing emails that pretend to be from Google or Microsoft

blocks.text: **[[encryption|Encryption]]** scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Cloud providers encrypt data while it's stored and while it travels over the internet (look for HTTPS).
Backups
A **[[backup]]** is a copy of data kept so it can be restored if the original is lost, deleted or locked by ransomware.

Syncing is not the same as backup. If a file syncs between your laptop and the cloud and you delete it (or ransomware scrambles it), the change syncs too, and both copies can be lost. Version history and separate backups protect you.

blocks.caption: The 3-2-1 backup rule
head: Number
Rule
Example
rows: Keep three copies of important data
On two different types of storage
A laptop drive and a cloud service
Cloud storage, or a drive kept at another house

blocks.text: Data sovereignty

**[[data sovereignty|Data sovereignty]]** means data is subject to the laws of the country where it's stored. Schools, hospitals and governments often need to know which country their cloud data is kept in, so they can make sure it's protected by UK data protection law.

blocks.title: Cloud security audit
steps: Read the profile of "Jordan's" cloud account: password used on 4 sites, no 2FA, 12 folders shared with "anyone with the link", no backups, phone is the only device.
Identify at least five risks.
Write a step-by-step plan to secure Jordan's account, in priority order.
Design a 3-2-1 backup plan for Jordan's photos and schoolwork.

q.a: Reused password; no 2FA; folders shared publicly; no backup; only one device; possibly old shared links never removed.
3 copies: phone, cloud photo backup and an external drive; 2 types of storage: phone/cloud and external drive; 1 off-site: the cloud copy.

check.q: In the shared responsibility model, who secures your password and sharing settings?
What is 2FA?
o: A second check, like a code on your phone, as well as a password

check.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule say?
Why is syncing not the same as backup?
o: Deletions and damage can sync to every copy

practice.a: Provider secures data centres/hardware/network (1); user secures accounts, passwords and sharing (1).

practice.q: Describe three ways to keep a cloud storage account secure.
practice.a: Any three: strong/unique password (1); 2FA (1); careful sharing settings (1); spot phishing (1); check activity alerts (1).

pages.title: The environmental cost
pages.spec: Describe the environmental impact of data centres, AI and devices, including energy, water and e-waste
pages.summary: Data centres use around 1-2% of the world's electricity, and AI is making demand grow quickly. They also use water for cooling, and making and throwing away devices creates carbon emissions and e-waste. Every digital action has a physical cost.
pages.starter: Does sending an email, streaming a video or asking an AI chatbot have an environmental cost? Rank them.
sc: I can describe how data centres affect the environment
I can explain why AI is increasing energy demand
I can describe the impact of making and disposing of devices

b: Data centres use roughly 1.5% of the world's electricity, and rising
AI is a major driver: training and running large models needs huge computing power
Forecasts suggest data centre electricity could roughly double by 2030
If electricity comes from fossil fuels, that means carbon emissions
Many data centres use water to cool servers
Large sites can use millions of litres a day
Concerns in places with water shortages
Data centres need land, grid connections and new power stations
Most of a phone's lifetime carbon comes from making it (embodied carbon)
Mining metals for chips and batteries harms environments
E-waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams in the world
Keeping devices longer is one of the biggest green actions

blocks.text: Energy use

Data centres use around 1.5% of the world's electricity, and demand is rising quickly as AI grows. The International Energy Agency has forecast that data centre electricity use could roughly double by 2030. Training a large AI model and answering millions of questions every day takes enormous computing power. If that electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, it adds to an organisation's **[[carbon footprint]]**: the total greenhouse gases its activities cause.

Big tech companies are investing heavily in **[[renewable energy]]** (wind, solar, hydro) and some are turning to nuclear power to supply their data centres, but demand is growing faster than clean supply in many places.
Water

Many data centres use water to cool servers, often by evaporating it. Large sites can use millions of litres per day, which raises concerns in areas with droughts or water shortages. Some newer designs use closed-loop liquid cooling that recycles water.
Devices and e-waste

blocks.caption: The life of a smartphone
head: Stage
Environmental impact
rows: Metals like cobalt, lithium and gold are mined, sometimes harming land, water and workers
Uses lots of energy; most of a phone's lifetime carbon comes from this stage (embodied carbon)
Charging and the data centres behind its apps
E-waste may contain toxic materials; valuable metals are lost if not recycled

blocks.text: **[[embodied carbon|Embodied carbon]]** is the carbon emitted making a product, before you ever switch it on. For a smartphone, it's typically most of the total. **[[e-waste|E-waste]]** (electronic waste) is one of the fastest-growing kinds of waste in the world, and only a small share is properly recycled.

The Republic of Ireland shows the scale of the issue: data centres now use around a fifth of all its electricity, more than all urban homes combined, leading to limits on new connections in the Dublin area.

blocks.title: Footprint detectives
steps: Use the (approximate) footprint cards for digital activities: an hour of HD streaming, an email with a big attachment, 10 AI chatbot questions, generating an AI image, making a new phone.
Rank them from lowest to highest impact.
Calculate your class's weekly streaming footprint using the card values.
Decide which single change would make the biggest difference.

q.q: Which activity has the biggest impact, and why?
q.a: Making a new phone, because of the energy and materials used in mining and manufacturing (embodied carbon), which outweigh years of everyday use.

q.q: Which single change makes the biggest difference?
q.a: Keeping devices longer (and repairing them) rather than upgrading often; then reducing unnecessary streaming quality and AI use.

check.q: Roughly what share of world electricity do data centres use?
Why is AI increasing data centre energy demand?
o: Training and running large models needs huge computing power

check.q: What is embodied carbon?
Why do some data centres use lots of water?

practice.q: Describe three ways data centres affect the environment.
practice.a: Any three: electricity use/carbon emissions (1); water for cooling (1); land use (1); e-waste from old servers (1); pressure on the grid (1).

practice.q: Explain why keeping a phone for longer is good for the environment.
practice.a: Most of a phone's carbon comes from manufacturing (1); fewer new phones made means less mining, energy and e-waste (1).

pages.title: Green computing
pages.spec: Describe how computing can be made greener by organisations, programmers and individuals
pages.summary: Green computing means designing, using and disposing of technology in ways that reduce its environmental impact. Data centres can use renewable energy and reuse waste heat, programmers can write efficient code, and everyone can keep devices longer, repair and recycle them, and use digital services thoughtfully. Technology can also help fight climate change.
pages.starter: Name one thing you could change about how you use technology this week to reduce its environmental impact.
sc: I can describe green computing actions for data centres
I can explain how efficient software reduces energy use
I can make a personal green computing plan

b: Power from renewable energy
Reuse waste heat to warm homes, offices, greenhouses and swimming pools
Efficient cooling, e.g. using cold outside air or liquid cooling
Carbon-aware computing: run big jobs when the grid is greenest
Efficient algorithms do the same job with fewer steps, so less energy
Smaller AI models can be good enough for many tasks
Compress images and videos; don't load what users don't need
Measure energy use, like any other bug to fix
Keep devices longer; repair, don't replace
Recycle e-waste properly; donate working devices
Turn off and unplug; use power-saving modes
Stream at lower quality on small screens; delete files you don't need

blocks.text: What is green computing?
**[[green computing|Green computing]]** means designing, making, using and disposing of technology in ways that reduce harm to the environment.
Greener data centres

blocks.title: How data centres are going green
items: Renewable energy: wind, solar and hydro power contracts
**[[heat reuse|Heat reuse]]**: piping waste heat to warm homes, offices or swimming pools (already done in Denmark, Finland and London)
Free cooling: using cold outside air in cooler climates
Liquid cooling: more efficient than air for powerful AI chips
**[[carbon-aware computing|Carbon-aware computing]]**: running big jobs (like AI training) at times or places where the grid has the most renewable power

blocks.text: Greener software

Software affects energy use too. An efficient algorithm does the same job in fewer steps, so it uses less processing power and electricity. Programmers can compress images and videos, avoid loading content users don't need, and choose smaller AI models when they're good enough.

blocks.title: Efficient search saves energy
blocks.context: A sorted list has 1,000,000 items. How many checks to find one item?
steps: Linear search checks items one by one: up to 1,000,000 checks.
Binary search halves the list each time: about 20 checks.
blocks.answer: Binary search uses about 50,000 times fewer steps, saving time and energy when run millions of times a day.

blocks.text: Greener you

blocks.caption: Personal green computing actions
head: Action
Why it helps
rows: Reduces mining, manufacturing and e-waste (the biggest impact)
**[[right to repair|Right to repair]]** laws in the UK and EU make spare parts easier to get
Recovers valuable materials; gives devices a second life
Lower screen brightness, sleep modes, switch off at night
Lower video quality on small screens; download music you play often
Delete unwanted files, photos and emails stored in the cloud

blocks.text: Tech for the planet

Technology can also help tackle climate change: smart grids balance renewable power, sensors monitor deforestation and pollution, AI improves weather forecasts and designs better batteries, and video calls can replace some travel.

blocks.title: Green tech pledge
steps: Audit your group's technology habits for a typical week (devices, streaming, storage, AI use, charging).
Choose three personal actions and one action the school could take.
Estimate the impact of each action using the footprint cards from last lesson.
Create a "green computing pledge" poster for your classroom.

q.q: Write your three personal actions and why you chose them.
q.a: E.g. keep my phone at least 4 years (biggest impact on embodied carbon); stream on lower quality on my phone; delete old photos and videos from cloud storage.

q.q: What action could the school take?
q.a: E.g. turn off computers and screens at the end of the day automatically; buy refurbished devices; set up an e-waste recycling collection; choose a cloud provider using renewable energy.

check.q: What is green computing?
o: Using technology in ways that reduce environmental harm

check.q: What is heat reuse?
o: Using data centre waste heat to warm buildings

check.q: How does efficient code save energy?
o: It does the job in fewer steps, using less processing

check.q: Which personal action has the biggest environmental benefit?

practice.q: Describe three ways a data centre could reduce its environmental impact.
practice.a: Any three: renewable energy (1); heat reuse (1); free/liquid cooling (1); carbon-aware scheduling (1); efficient hardware/virtualisation (1).
Running big computing jobs (1) at times/places when the electricity grid has the most renewable power (1).
